title: The basilica
hook: early churches borrowed the Roman hall, a long nave to an apse

segments.voice: Yesterday, vows: a paper laid on an altar, poverty, chastity and obedience, or a Benedictine's stability. Your line was given wholly.

The heavy door swings shut, and the traffic noise is gone. Ahead stretches a long, straight floor. Columns march down both sides in two rows, like trees along a country road. Light falls in from high windows. And far away, at the very end, the wall curves into a half-circle, glowing with gold mosaic, an altar standing in front of it. This room wants anyone in it to go one way: forward. A whole church, shaped like a road. Today: the basilica.

The block turns from rites to spaces, starting with a building borrowed from Rome. First, the hall. Historians describe the Roman basilica as a big public building for law courts and business: a long central hall, columns down each side, and at the far end a rounded space called the apse, where an official sat to hear cases. Second, the choice. When Christians began building large churches, historians point out, they didn't copy the temples around them. A Roman temple was a house for a god's statue, and the crowd mostly stayed outside. Christian worship needed the crowd inside, hearing the word and sharing the table, and the public hall had room. Third, the furniture. The long hall became the nave, where the people stand or sit. In the apse, where an official's seat had been, came the bishop's chair and, before it, the altar. A room built for judgment became a room built for worship, with a table at the end of the road. Fourth, the walk. The shape makes a path, door to altar, and people walk it: in processions, a bride up the aisle, people coming forward to receive communion. The psalms sing that movement: "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise." And: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Hebrews uses the same picture for coming near to God: "boldness to enter into the holiest" by "a new and living way." Some churches built since, even ones that look nothing like Rome, still keep the long walk.
screen: `A ROMAN HALL FOR COURTS AND BUSINESS.`
`DOOR TO ALTAR: A PATH TO WALK.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly to the front of a church, or, if you can't get to one, walk it in your mind: start at the door, one step on each slow breath, no hurry. When you arrive, stand still a moment. If you pray, say the psalm's line, I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD; if you don't, simply stand there and look.
The basilica. A long Roman hall borrowed for worship: a nave for the people, an apse with the altar, and a path between.
Your line: the long walk. Door to altar. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Some churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, keep the basilica's long plan: a nave where the congregation gathers and a central aisle leading to the altar or communion table, walked in processions, at weddings and when people come forward to receive communion.

chat.says: Why are so many old churches long and narrow, like a hallway?
options: They borrowed the Roman basilica, a public hall with room for a crowd to walk to the altar.
They copied Roman temples, which were built long so worshippers could fill them inside.
It was cheaper to build that way; the shape has no meaning for how people worship.
chat.meaning: Christians borrowed Rome's public hall, not its temples, because worship needed the crowd inside. The shape makes a path from door to altar.

basilica.meaning: a long Roman public hall, borrowed for churches
